module.objective: Mampu menggunakan present tenses dan future tenses untuk membicarakan rencana hidup, ambisi, dan perubahan kebiasaan dengan percaya diri

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Life Plans, Ambitions, and Habits

subModules.vocabularyFocus: Resolutions, Lifestyle Choices, and Career Goals

content.summary: Welcome to the first reading mission of level B2. In this lesson, you will explore texts about personal ambitions, New Year resolutions, and changing habits. You will learn how English speakers use different present and future tense forms to discuss future plans, ongoing struggles, and fixed arrangements.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present Simple, Present Continuous, Present Perfect, Present Perfect Continuous, and Future forms.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Vocabulary related to making resolutions, breaking bad habits, and planning professional careers.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming texts for general meaning and scanning paragraphs to identify specific grammar patterns and time markers.

learningObjectives: Understand the main ideas of B2 level texts discussing life plans and habit formation.
Locate specific details regarding personal goals, timetables, and recurring complaints.
Recognize and apply correct tense structures when expressing future arrangements and ongoing actions.

contextWarmup.prompt: When people make New Year resolutions, what is the most common reason they stop trying after a few weeks?
options: They set goals that are too difficult or unrealistic.
They forget what their resolution was on the first day.
They prefer to write their goals down in a diary instead.
contextWarmup.explanation: Setting overly ambitious goals without a clear, gradual plan is the primary reason people struggle and eventually give up on their resolutions.

rules: Present Simple is used for permanent situations, general facts, and regular opinions.
Present Continuous expresses temporary actions happening now, annoying habits with 'always', or fixed future arrangements.
Present Perfect Continuous highlights an action that started in the past and is still continuing right now.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Present Continuous and Present Simple for Future
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often mix up timetables with personal arrangements. Remember that timetables use Present Simple, while personal plans use Present Continuous.
commonTrap.wrong: I meet my careers advisor tomorrow at 10 AM, so I must prepare.
commonTrap.correct: I am meeting my careers advisor tomorrow at 10 AM, because we arranged it yesterday.

content.passageTitle: New Year, New Me: Reality Versus Ambition
paragraphs: Every January, millions of people around the world make a resolution to transform their lives. They promise themselves they will go to the gym every single day, eat organic vegetables, and completely break their bad habits. However, reality often strikes very quickly. By the middle of February, many individuals are struggling with their schedules and have already given up on their ambitious goals. Psychologists explain that making drastic changes overnight rarely works because human brains prefer small, consistent steps over sudden shocks.

On the other hand, some people manage to form lasting good habits by focusing on realistic targets. Maya, a university student in London, decided to approach her life plans differently this year. Instead of saying she will change everything at once, she is taking a course in time management and meeting her academic advisor tomorrow afternoon to discuss her career path. Maya believes that staying organized and setting clear milestones will help her get promoted in her future job and eventually settle down without feeling overwhelmed.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Managing Busy Schedules and Life Plans

content.summary: When listening to native speakers talk about busy schedules, pay close attention to present tenses used for fixed timetables and future forms used for intentions. Notice how words run together in fast speech, often dropping certain consonant sounds.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about weekly schedules and personal ambitions.
Identify specific details such as days of the week, activities, and personal preferences.
Notice how words link together in connected speech during casual teenage chats.

connectedSpeech.note: The auxiliary verb 'do you' reduces to 'dyu' in fast spoken English.
Linking the final consonant of 'give' to the vowel in 'it'.
The 't' in what and 'is' combine to sound like 's'.
Standard casual reduction of want to before a verb.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Expressing Life Plans and Future Ambitions

content.summary: Mastering present and future tenses allows you to articulate career goals, personal ambitions, and ongoing lifestyle changes with precision and clarity at the B2 level.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Stating Current Ambitions and Facts
blueprintItems.example: I want to secure a promotion by the end of this year.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Describing Ongoing Self-Improvement
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Present Perfect Continuous + Verb-ing + Time Marker
blueprintItems.example: I have been training for the marathon for three months now.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Outlining Future Fixed Arrangements and Plans
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + Present Continuous or 'be going to' + Future Time Expression
blueprintItems.example: I am meeting my career advisor on Tuesday morning to discuss my promotion.

mechanicsRules.rule: Avoid mixing informal contractions in formal life plan essays.
mechanicsRules.badExample: gonna launch my own business next year.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I am going to launch my own business next year.
mechanicsRules.why: Formal writing requires full grammatical structures instead of colloquial slang.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize specific months, professional titles, and names of institutions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: i will start working at microsoft in september.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I will start working at Microsoft in September.
mechanicsRules.why: Proper nouns and proper adjectives must always begin with an uppercase letter.

mechanicsRules.rule: Ensure correct punctuation when using time clauses for future events.
mechanicsRules.badExample: When I graduate I will move abroad.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: When I graduate, I will move abroad.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma is required after an introductory dependent time clause.

sampleSentences.en: I am hoping to transition into digital marketing within the next six months.
sampleSentences.id: Saya berharap dapat beralih ke pemasaran digital dalam enam bulan ke depan.

sampleSentences.en: We are flying to Berlin next Friday for the international tech conference.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Career Goals and Ambitions
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences detailing your professional ambitions. State your current position, what you are doing to advance, and your future plans for next year.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I currently work as a junior developer. I have been taking advanced coding classes for three months. Next year, I am going to apply for a senior engineer position.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Lifestyle Changes and Routine Adjustments
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences describing a recent change in your lifestyle. Explain how long you have been maintaining this habit and what your future expectation is.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I have started waking up at five o'clock every morning. I am currently trying to improve my daily productivity. I believe this habit will help me achieve my long-term goals.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the present continuous tense to express an annoying habit:
practicumQuestions.promptText: My colleague always interrupts me during team meetings.
targetAnswers: My colleague is always interrupting me during team meetings.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present continuous with 'always' is used to express irritation about repeated actions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the present perfect continuous tense:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I started practicing the piano three hours ago and I am still playing.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'have been practicing for three hours'.
targetAnswers: I have been practicing the piano for three hours.
I have been practicing the piano for three hours now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Present perfect continuous describes an action that started in the past and continues into the present.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Combine the two sentences using 'by the time':
practicumQuestions.promptText: I finish university. I will have mastered two foreign languages.
practicumQuestions.hint: Place 'By the time' at the beginning of the sentence.
targetAnswers: By the time I finish university, I will have mastered two foreign languages.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When the time clause starts the sentence, a comma separates it from the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct all punctuation, capitalization, and grammar errors in the sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: next month i am moving to london to start a new job
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize 'Next', 'I', and 'London'. Add a period at the end.
targetAnswers: Next month, I am moving to London to start a new job.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns (London), sentence beginnings, and first-person pronouns require capitalization.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence describing a fixed future arrangement for next week using the present continuous tense:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Arrangement: Dentist appointment on Thursday at 10 AM.
practicumQuestions.hint: Example: I am visiting the dentist on Thursday morning.
targetAnswers: I am seeing the dentist on Thursday morning.
I am visiting the dentist on Thursday.
I am having a dentist appointment on Thursday.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present continuous is ideal for formal arrangements and scheduled appointments.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following affirmative sentence into a negative future sentence using 'be going to':
practicumQuestions.promptText: She is going to accept the job offer.
targetAnswers: She is not going to accept the job offer.
She isn't going to accept the job offer.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Negation in future plans with 'be going to' is formed by placing 'not' after the auxiliary verb 'is'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a sentence using the present perfect tense to express an unspecific past action relevant now:
practicumQuestions.hint: Example: I have applied for the scholarship.
targetAnswers: I have applied for the scholarship.
I have already applied for the scholarship.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The present perfect connects past actions to present relevance without specifying an exact time.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using 'will' for a spontaneous decision:
practicumQuestions.promptText: My laptop battery is dying. (Make a decision to plug it in immediately)
targetAnswers: I will plug it in right now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Will' is used for instant decisions made at the moment of speaking.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the error in verb tense selection:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I am knowing the answer to your question.
practicumQuestions.hint: Stative verbs like 'know' are not typically used in continuous tenses.
targetAnswers: I know the answer to your question.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Stative verbs expressing mental states, such as 'know', use the present simple instead of the present continuous.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complex sentence expressing a life ambition using 'so that':
practicumQuestions.promptText: Ambition: Save money / buy an apartment.
practicumQuestions.hint: Example: I am saving money so that I can buy an apartment.
targetAnswers: I am saving money so that I can buy an apartment.
I save money so that I can buy an apartment.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'So that' introduces a clause of purpose, explaining the motivation behind an action.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Life Plans, Resolutions, and Future Ambitions

content.summary: This module focuses on articulating future plans and personal resolutions clearly at a B2 CEFR level. You will master syllable stress in multi-syllable ambition vocabulary, sentence rhythm when discussing timelines, and polite intonation patterns during interactive roleplay scenarios.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to word stress shifts when changing word forms, such as moving from the verb 'resolve' to the noun 'resolution'. Keep your voice projection steady and ensure sentence-final intonation falls naturally on declarative statements about your future goals.

pillars.name: Primary Word Stress
pillars.target: Accurate placement of primary stress in multi-syllable vocabulary
pillars.explanation: English relies heavily on syllable prominence. Words like resolution, ambition, and commitment require a clear, lengthened primary stressed syllable while reducing unstressed vowels to schwa sounds.

pillars.name: Sentence Rhythm
pillars.target: Linking content words and compressing function words
pillars.explanation: Speak with natural pacing by stressing content verbs and nouns while smoothly blending auxiliary verbs and prepositions together in connected speech.

pillars.name: Intonation Contours
pillars.target: Using rising and falling tones to convey certainty and inquiry
pillars.explanation: Use a falling tone for definite life plans and fixed schedules. Use a rising tone when asking clarifying questions about other people's ambitions during conversations.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The primary stress shifts from the second syllable in the verb 'resolve' to the third syllable in the noun 'resolution'.
Both the noun and adjective maintain primary stress on the second syllable, but the vowel quality changes slightly.
The base verb 'retire' stresses the second syllable, and adding the suffix '-ment' keeps the main stress on the same root syllable.
The verb 'promote' places stress on the second syllable, while the noun 'promotion' shifts the primary stress to the third syllable.

drills.targetText: I made a firm resolution to break bad habits this year.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ meɪd ə fɜːm ˌrezəˈluːʃən tuː breɪk bæd ˈhæbɪts ðɪs jɪə/
drills.focus: Noun collocation 'made a resolution' and clear syllable stress
drills.hint: Ensure the word resolution has a distinct secondary stress on the first syllable and primary stress on the third.

drills.targetText: She is struggling with her new routine and might give up.
drills.phonetic: /ʃiː ɪz ˈstrʌɡəlɪŋ wɪð hɜː nuː ruːˈtiːn ænd maɪt ɡɪv ʌp/
drills.focus: Continuous verb phrasing and phrasal verb linking
drills.hint: Link 'struggling with' smoothly and pronounce 'give up' as a single connected unit.

drills.targetText: By next month, he hopes to get promoted and settle down.
drills.phonetic: /baɪ nekst mʌnθ, hiː həʊps tuː ɡet prəˈməʊtɪd ænd ˈsetəl daʊn/
drills.focus: Future time marker rhythm and phrasal verb articulation
drills.hint: Pause slightly after the time marker 'By next month' before delivering the main clause.

drills.targetText: Many ambitious workers plan to retire early and travel abroad.
drills.phonetic: /ˈmeni æmˈbɪʃəs ˈwɜːkəz plæn tuː rɪˈtaɪə ˈɜːli ænd ˈtrævəl əˈbrɔːd/
drills.focus: Adjective stress and compound verb pacing
drills.hint: Emphasize the adjectives 'ambitious' and 'early' to give your sentence natural spoken texture.
